name: Ambedkarism
summary: Ambedkarism here is B. R. Ambedkar's own political thought: abolition of caste by destroying the shastras' authority, liberty, equality and fraternity as the governing principles, constitutional parliamentary democracy with enforceable rights and group safeguards, and a state-led economy that he put most firmly in 1947 and left more open in 1951. He rejected violence and dictatorship as means, saw social democracy as the condition of political democracy, and ended in a rationalist Buddhism.
scope: Ambedkar's own thought only, from his writings, speeches, party manifestos and record: Annihilation of Caste (1936), States and Minorities (1947), the Constituent Assembly speeches, Buddha or Karl Marx (1956), the Scheduled Castes Federation manifesto (1951), his Hindu Code Bill speeches, resignation statement and Bombay and Central Assembly labour record. No later organisation (BSP, RPI factions, Dalit Panthers, Ambedkarite NGOs) and no other ideology (Marxism, liberalism, Buddhism in general) is borrowed. Where his early and late texts differ (state socialism 1947 against the 1951 'no dogma' manifesto; penalising shastric preaching in 1936 against freedom to preach in 1947), the answer is low.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: He argues in States and Minorities that private enterprise cannot industrialise India and that liberty from state control is 'the dictatorship of the private employer', but his 1951 manifesto allows private enterprise wherever national undertaking is not essential.

public-ownership.rationale: His 1947 States and Minorities memorandum has the state own and run key and basic industries; his 1951 Scheduled Castes Federation manifesto backs national undertaking 'where possible and essential', nationalised insurance and state river-valley power, but also lets private enterprise run what is not essential.

property-fundamental.rationale: States and Minorities protects property from deprivation without due process but subordinates it to constitutionally mandated state ownership of land and industry (with debenture compensation).

regulate-corporations.rationale: States and Minorities makes discrimination by private employers an offence, and the 1951 manifesto says any scheme of production must involve 'no exploitation of the working classes'.

cut-welfare.rationale: His constitutional preamble commits the state to give every subject freedom from want, and States and Minorities makes the state responsible for capital, insurance and livelihood.

missingStatements.declined: Specific to one country's caste law; covered by equal-moral-worth.

missingStatements.text: Social boycott of a group, and threatening or promoting it, should be a criminal offence.
missingStatements.rationale: States and Minorities proposes making social boycott, instigating it and threatening it cognizable offences, to protect the Untouchables from economic and social pressure.
missingStatements.declined: Specific to one country's caste law.

notes: Written from the primary volumes (Writings and Speeches, Government of Maharashtra editions via archive.org) read in full text; the 1937 Independent Labour Party manifesto was not found in the text, so the party's record comes from the Bombay Assembly speeches. Economy is the main tension: States and Minorities (1947) makes state ownership of key industries and collective farming constitutional, the 1951 manifesto says no dogma and allows private enterprise where national undertaking is not essential, and Buddha or Karl Marx (1956) keeps abolition of private property as the lasting part of Marx; these are answered low or medium. The Roham birth-control speech in Vol. 2 is not used (Roham says he delivered Ambedkar's points); birth control rests on the 1951 manifesto. Strict strand rule needed no strands: Ambedkarism here is one thinker.
